query: According to episode 7, why can no machine decide in general whether an arbitrary program halts?
answer:
Turing shows that a “checker” that could tell, for any machine + input, whether it will eventually halt cannot exist. He starts by **assuming** such a checker exists and then builds a new machine (the “troublemaker”) that uses the checker as a sub‑routine. The troublemaker feeds its own description to the checker and then does the opposite of whatever answer it receives: if the checker says the machine halts, the troublemaker loops forever; if the checker says it runs forever, the troublemaker halts. When we give the troublemaker its own description, whichever answer the checker gives leads to a contradiction—its prediction is always wrong. Because this self‑referential construction forces the checker to give a false answer, no consistent halting‑decision procedure can exist. Hence **no machine can decide in general whether an arbitrary program halts**. 

- “No machine can decide in general whether an arbitrary machine halts. The halting problem is undecidable… impossible in the strongest sense, a theorem proven” (Episode 7, 26:22‑27:51).  
- The proof proceeds by assuming a checker, building a troublemaker that “deliberately does the opposite of the answer,” and showing that feeding the troublemaker its own description makes the checker wrong in either case (Episode 7, 24:54‑26:21).  
- The contradiction is set up by “suppose the checker exists… the same flavor as the old liar’s paradox” (Episode 7, 23:24‑24:54).
